title: What Do Teachers ACTUALLY Need to Know?
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer opens by noting that the relationship between teachers' own subject-matter math knowledge and their students' achievement gains is surprisingly weak, which has led researchers like Ball and Hill to investigate more specialized forms of teacher knowledge. He centers the piece on knowledge of student misconceptions (KOSM): a study that gave students and teachers the same multiple-choice science assessment found teachers had strong subject-matter knowledge (84.5% correct) but were weak at identifying the most common wrong answer on misconception-heavy items (42.7%). The most striking finding, Meyer reports, is that student gains were only significantly larger when teachers had both subject-matter knowledge and knowledge of misconceptions -- subject-matter knowledge alone made no significant difference. He frames his own professional project -- building curriculum that invites visible student thinking, and tools that give teachers visibility into that thinking -- as an attempt to help teachers develop this specific, underrated form of expertise at scale. Meyer closes with a roundup of adjacent items, including skepticism toward a Wired story claiming teachers are "going all in" on generative AI, based on the story quoting only one actual teacher.
points: Meyer highlights a striking asymmetry: teachers averaged 84.5% correct on subject-matter items but only 42.7% at identifying the single most common wrong answer on misconception items.
Student achievement gains were significantly larger only when a teacher had both subject-matter knowledge and knowledge of student misconceptions -- subject-matter knowledge alone was not enough.

Meyer's own theory of change centers on this gap: build curriculum that invites visible student thinking, then build tools that give teachers visibility into that thinking, particularly around common wrong answers.

He flags a Wired article claiming teachers are "going all in" on generative AI as thin evidence, noting it quotes school leaders, founders, researchers, and venture capitalists but only one actual classroom teacher.
quotes: It is conventional wisdom that teachers need to know what they're teaching in order to teach it well. But the relationship between teacher knowledge of math (measured by post-secondary coursework, for example) and student achievement gains is surprisingly strained.
Teacher SMK (subject matter knowledge) performance on the pretest was strong, with 84.5% correct on non-misconception items and 82.5% on misconception items.

Teachers' KOSM, the ability to identify the most common wrong answer on misconception items, was weak, with an average score of 42.7% identified, averaging only 5 out of the 12 items with strong misconceptions.

Students of teachers who had only SMK on an item had gains that were not significantly different from those of students who had teachers without SMK. Only when teachers had both SMK and KOSM were student gains significantly larger.
My instinct about generative AI in education is the opposite of this Wired headline, "Teachers Are Going All In on Generative AI," so I read it with a lot of interest.
